title: [Thesis Defense] Robots That Think Before They Act: Planning and Perception for Generalizable Manipulation
description: [Thesis Defense] Robots That Think Before They Act: Planning and Perception for Generalizable Manipulation Location: 32-D463 (Star)Title: Robots That Think Before They Act: Planning and Perception for Generalizable ManipulationAbstract: A home robot will encounter a wide variety of objects, instructions, and environments it has never seen before. No amount of engineering or data collection can cover every situation. This defense argues that handling this variety is a problem of composition, and that planning provides the mechanism, allowing the robot to think before it acts. I develop this idea across three areas: planning by scaling test-time compute, planning from perception, and planning to guide perception. We first develop a task and motion planner that combines compositional sampling with differentiable optimization on GPUs, refining thousands of candidate solutions in parallel to solve tightly constrained problems in seconds. We then integrate our planner with foundation models for perception and language into a complete tabletop manipulation system. This system uses no task-specific robot data, yet outperforms state-of-the-art learned policies on long-horizon and semantic reasoning tasks. Finally, we turn to mobile manipulation with an agent that grounds objects and concepts from raw observations on the fly, reasons over spatial and semantic relations, and checks feasibility before acting. Every method runs on multiple real robots, from tabletop arms to mobile manipulators.Thesis Committee: Leslie Pack Kaelbling (thesis advisor), Tomás Lozano-Pérez (thesis advisor), Phillip Isola TBD August 31, 2026 Massive Parallelization of Irregular Computations: Parallel Algorithm Design and Hardware Acceleration Dayi Fan The Ohio State University 2:00 P - 3:00 P Location 32-G575

title: THESIS DEFENSE (NICHOLAS PFAFF)
description: THESIS DEFENSE (NICHOLAS PFAFF): Generating Simulation-Ready Worlds for Robot Learning and Evaluation THESIS DEFENSE (NICHOLAS PFAFF): Generating Simulation-Ready Worlds for Robot Learning and EvaluationSpeaker: Nicholas PfaffSpeaker Affiliation: MIT CSAILHost: Prof. Russ TedrakeHost Affiliation: MIT CSAILZoom Link: TBDAbstract: General-purpose robots must operate across the diversity of real homes and workplaces. Much of the recent progress toward this goal comes from learned robot policies, including vision-language-action models trained on large datasets and GPU clusters. Developing these policies increasingly follows the experimental workflow of other machine-learning fields: train a model, evaluate it, and use the result to choose the next experiment. Training throughput can grow with GPU compute. Evaluation still often requires human operators to prepare scenes, reset robots, supervise rollouts, and record outcomes, so its throughput remains limited by robot time and human supervision. Simulation could make routine evaluation another compute job, but a simulator can only test policies in the worlds it is given. Today, those worlds are often hand-authored, sparse, static, or missing the physical structure required for contact-rich interaction. Creating diverse, simulation-ready content is therefore the bottleneck addressed in this thesis. This thesis develops methods for generating simulation-ready content at increasing scale, from individual object assets to cluttered arrangements to complete indoor environments. Simulation-ready content contains separable objects, collision geometry, physical properties, feasible placements, and export paths into robot simulators. The central question is how to produce this content automatically while still approximating the diversity and physical complexity of the real world. Scalable Real2Sim turns robot interaction with real objects into simulation-ready assets, reconstructing geometry and identifying inertial properties without custom scanning hardware or manual measurement. Steerable Scene Generation learns a generative prior over cluttered SE(3) object arrangements from large-scale proxy scene data, then adapts that prior through conditioning, post-training, and inference-time search toward robot-relevant objectives. SceneSmith generates complete indoor environments from language. It uses vision-language-model agents to design, critique, and revise scenes, while an integrated pipeline handles asset generation, articulated-object retrieval, physical property estimation, and physics-based feasibility checks. SceneSmith also connects generated environments to policy rollout and automatic scoring. The systems obtain their knowledge of the real world from physical interaction with real objects, imperfect but scalable scene data, and internet-trained vision-language models. They turn that knowledge into simulation-ready worlds that can be generated as part of the same compute-driven workflow used for policy training. These worlds make it possible to run more routine evaluation as compute jobs, allowing robotics experiments to scale without proportional growth in robots and human operators.Thesis committee: Russ Tedrake (Thesis Supervisor), Phillip Isola (Thesis Reader), Tomás Lozano-Pérez (Thesis Reader) TBD September 4, 2026 Thesis Defense: Efficient, Diverse and Reliable Sampling from Language Models Theo Olausson MIT-CSAIL 10:00 A - 12:00 P Location 32-G882 Hewlett
